steps.prompt: The worksheet is filled. Four programs require a course you cannot fit before submission. Three require the GRE, which you have not taken and do not want to take. Two are on probationary accreditation. One states a hard cumulative minimum of `3.4`.

choices.text: Run the hard filter pass and cut all ten, since each is disqualifying on arithmetic rather than on judgment
choices.feedback: Correct, with one nuance. A prerequisite you truly cannot fit and a hard GPA minimum are absolute. The GRE is a choice, so decide it once: if three programs are worth the exam, take it; if not, cut them and stop reconsidering.

choices.text: Keep everything and decide later, since cutting early narrows options
choices.feedback: Carrying disqualified programs costs application fees, supplemental fees, and essay time on files that cannot be admitted. The hard filter exists to spend that effort where it can work.

choices.text: Cut only the probationary programs and keep the rest as reaches
choices.feedback: A reach means your numbers are below the average, not that you fail a stated requirement. A missing prerequisite is a rejection before the file is read.

steps.prompt: Ten programs remain. Checking your numbers against each published class profile, you are below the average GPA at seven of them, roughly matching at two, and above at one. Your hours are well above average at all ten.

choices.text: Add programs that weigh patient care experience heavily and programs that calculate a last-60-credit GPA, to build a bucket where your profile scores well
choices.feedback: Correct. Your upward trend over 40 credits is invisible to a program that only reads a cumulative GPA, and fully visible to one calculating recent credits. That is the exact category to add.

choices.text: Apply to all ten anyway, since volume compensates for fit
choices.feedback: Ten programs that all score the same way turn one weakness into ten rejections. Volume without variation in scoring does not improve the odds much.

choices.text: Delay the application by a year to raise the cumulative GPA above the averages
choices.feedback: Sometimes right, often not. Moving a cumulative GPA takes many credits, and a year of delay is a year of tuition and lost earnings. Look first for programs whose scoring already rewards the trend you have.

steps.prompt: You settle on nine programs: one where you are above the class average, three matching, three below, and two that use a last-60-credit calculation. Four require a supplemental application, two require a PA letter specifically, and one requires CASPer.

choices.text: Record every program-specific requirement with its fee and deadline in the worksheet, and re-verify each row next spring
choices.feedback: Correct. A missed supplemental silently ends an otherwise competitive application, and the requirements are exactly the fields that change between cycles. The worksheet is the only place this information survives.

choices.text: Trust that CASPA will prompt you for anything program-specific
choices.feedback: Program Materials surfaces many requirements, but supplementals sent by the program's own email and situational tests arranged separately are easy to miss during a busy cycle.

choices.text: Drop the CASPer program to avoid the extra test
choices.feedback: Defensible if the program is a poor fit anyway, and a poor reason on its own. CASPer is a few hours, and dropping a well-matched program to avoid it is a bad trade.

scenarios.debrief: The list-building method is three passes, in order, and the order is what does the work. The hard filter pass is arithmetic: a missing prerequisite, a hard GPA minimum, a required test you will not take, or an accreditation status you will not accept. Those are rejections before the file is read, and carrying them costs fees and essay time. The soft filter pass is where a specific profile gets matched to a specific scoring system, and it is the pass most applicants skip. An upward trend across recent credits is invisible to a program reading only a cumulative GPA and decisive at a program calculating the last 60. Strong hours are decisive at a program that weighs experience and nearly irrelevant at one that does not. Finally, everything on the worksheet has a shelf life of about one year. Prerequisites, deadlines, test requirements and accreditation status all change, which is why the last step is a calendar reminder for the spring of the application year.

scenarios.title: The cycle, decision by decision
scenarios.intro: It is March. CASPA opens in late April. You will finish your last prerequisite in May, you have nine programs on the list, about 4,400 documented patient care hours with roughly 700 more projected before matriculation, and three letter writers in mind. Every decision from here is about sequence.

steps.prompt: You have not asked anyone for a letter yet. Your three intended writers are a PA you have worked alongside for two years, your charge nurse, and the professor from your microbiology course last fall.

choices.text: Ask all three in person this week, asking specifically whether they can write a strong letter, and hand each a packet with your resume, hours, program list and the deadline
choices.feedback: Correct on timing and on wording. Six to eight weeks before you need them is now, and asking for a strong letter gives a lukewarm writer a graceful way to decline, which is a favor to you.

choices.text: Enter them in CASPA when the portal opens and let the system email them
choices.feedback: The system email is the mechanism, not the request. A cold automated email to someone who was never asked in person is how letters sit unanswered for six weeks.

choices.text: Ask in June once the rest of the application is finished
choices.feedback: Letters are the one component another person controls, which makes them the thing you start earliest. June requests routinely land in August, which is past the window that matters.

steps.prompt: The portal opens. You have credits from three institutions: a community college, a four-year university, and one summer course taken in 2014 at a school you attended for a single term.

choices.text: Request official transcripts from all three immediately, including the 2014 summer school, and consider paying for Professional Transcript Entry
choices.feedback: Correct. Every institution ever attended must be listed, omission is an integrity problem, and verification cannot start until every transcript arrives. With three institutions, the transcript entry service is usually worth the fee.

choices.text: List the two main institutions and skip the single summer course, since it is old and irrelevant
choices.feedback: This is the one error on the list that is not recoverable. CASPA finds omitted institutions, and an omission is treated as an integrity issue rather than an oversight.

choices.text: Enter coursework from unofficial copies now and request official transcripts later
choices.feedback: Entering from an unofficial copy risks mismatches that return the file for correction, and delaying the requests delays the only thing that gates verification.

steps.prompt: It is early May. Coursework is entered, two letters are in, the third is pending, and your final prerequisite grade will not post until the end of the month. A friend advises waiting until everything is complete and perfect before submitting.

choices.text: Submit now with the spring course in progress and one letter pending, so verification starts, and confirm how each program treats in-progress prerequisites
choices.feedback: Correct. Verification takes two to six weeks and cannot start until you submit and the transcripts arrive. Waiting three weeks for a grade pushes the file into the crowded part of the cycle for no gain.

choices.text: Wait until the final grade posts and the third letter arrives, then submit in June
choices.feedback: This is the single most common self-inflicted injury in a rolling cycle. Three weeks of waiting plus four weeks of verification puts the file in front of programs in July instead of June.

choices.text: Submit to three programs now and add the rest later once everything is final
choices.feedback: Adding programs later is allowed, and it is not a reason to hold the other six. There is no benefit to submitting a partial list when the same verification covers all nine.

steps.prompt: Verification completes on June 12. Four of your nine programs require a supplemental application with its own fee and essays, and two of those arrive by email from the program rather than through CASPA.

choices.text: Work the supplementals within days, tracking each against the worksheet, and check email daily for the rest of the cycle
choices.feedback: Correct. A missed supplemental silently ends an application that was otherwise competitive, and program-sent emails are the ones most easily lost. The worksheet is what keeps four separate processes visible.

choices.text: Complete them over the next two months, since the program deadlines are in the autumn
choices.feedback: The program deadline is not the review date. A supplemental submitted in August means the file is read in August, which in a rolling cycle is a materially different class to compete for.

choices.text: Complete the two that came through CASPA and assume the emailed ones are optional
choices.feedback: Supplementals sent directly by a program are requirements, not invitations. Two applications would simply stop moving with no notification that anything was missing.

scenarios.debrief: The whole cycle is a sequencing problem. Three things gate everything else, and all three depend on other people, which is why they start first: letters, transcripts, and verification. Letters are requested in person six to eight weeks ahead with the word strong in the question. Transcripts are requested from every institution ever attended, without exception, because one missing document holds the entire file and an omitted school is an integrity finding rather than an oversight. Verification then takes two to six weeks and cannot begin until the application, the payment and all transcripts have arrived. Everything after that is calendar discipline. Submitting with a spring course in progress and one letter pending is normal and correct, because the alternative is trading a real place in a rolling queue for a cosmetic completeness nobody rewards. And supplementals, especially the ones a program emails directly, are requirements that fail silently. The pattern to carry: in a rolling cycle, the cost of waiting is never zero, and it is always paid in seats.
